_comment: the .NET platform REVIEW-SURFACES import — rules encoded in .claude/agents/architecture-reviewer.md (pattern checklist), .coderabbit.yaml path_instructions, and .claude/audits/ verdicts, deduped against dotnet-canon.json and dotnet-decisions.json. These are the rules the repo's automated reviewers enforce; porting them means another repo's agent learns them at check time instead of at review time. Review, then `okl seed seed/dotnet-review-surfaces.json`.

triggers: Adding a new minimal API endpoint for listing customer orders in the Ordering service.
Spinning up a new microservice and wiring up its HTTP routes with API versioning.
Reviewing a PR that adds an admin-only group of endpoints to the catalog API.
Refactoring how each service sets up its /api/v1 route prefixes, since every one does it slightly differently.
Pen test found an internal endpoint answering requests with no bearer token at all.
A list endpoint returned 50,000 rows when someone passed pageSize=100000 in the query string.
One service's endpoints show up under the wrong version in Swagger while the other services look fine.
route group conventions for ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, MapGroup with versioning and authorization
pagination limits, max page size, cap on results per request for REST list endpoints
anonymous access by accident, missing [Authorize] on an endpoint, unauthenticated API route
nodes.title: Endpoints register via the shared versioned-group helper, with group-level auth and server-side paging clamps
nodes.body: Every HTTP endpoint registers via MapV1ApiGroup(tag, name) instead of hand-rolled versioning chains, non-public groups get RequireAuthorization at the group level, and every list endpoint accepts (page, pageSize) clamped server-side at ≤100. Centralizing the policy in one helper makes per-service drift structurally impossible.
nodes.symptom: a new endpoint hand-rolls versioning, is anonymously reachable, or returns an uncapped list
nodes.fix: register on the versioned group helper, require auth at group level, clamp pageSize server-side

triggers: Writing an EF Core query that loads orders with their line items and shipments for a details page.
Optimizing a slow read endpoint that eager-loads several child collections of an aggregate.
Reviewing a PR that adds AsNoTracking to every read query to speed them up.
Building the read side for an order history screen backed by Entity Framework.
The SQL for this query returns thousands of rows for one order with twenty items and ten payments.
Getting duplicate parent objects in the result, one per child row, after adding another Include.
EF Core logs a warning about loading multiple collection navigations in a single query.
cartesian product blow-up when joining several one-to-many relations in an ORM
eager loading related data, N+1 versus one giant join, Hibernate fetch join duplicates
row explosion from JOINs, duplicated entities, identity resolution with no-tracking queries
nodes.title: Cartesian explosion has two axes — only projection-to-DTO fixes both; plain AsNoTracking is a half-fix
nodes.body: Include-based reads suffer client-side object duplication (fixed by identity-resolution tracking variants) AND cartesian SQL row shape (fixed only by projection or split queries). AsNoTracking returning an entity fixes neither the wire shape nor duplication. Inline projection to a DTO with nested collections wins on both axes at once — which is why it's the default read shape; identity-resolution no-tracking is the narrow fallback for materializing an untracked entity graph.
nodes.symptom: a read path materializing entities with Include, duplicating parents per child row
nodes.fix: project inline to a DTO with nested collections; the ORM auto-splits projected collection navigations

triggers: Implementing a feature that emails every subscriber when a new product drops.
Writing a message handler that pushes notifications to all members of a team when a project changes.
Reviewing a handler that loops over recipients and sends an SMS to each one inline.
Adding an endpoint that broadcasts an announcement to the admins of every tenant.
The send-announcement request times out once the mailing list grows past a few thousand people.
Whenever marketing sends a blast, CPU on one pod pegs and the rest of the system slows down.
The notify-all API call takes minutes to return because it waits for every email to go out.
fan-out to many users, mass notification, bulk send from a single handler
await inside a foreach loop, sequential sends, latency multiplied by the number of recipients
notification storm, sending to a big distribution list straight from an API call
nodes.title: Broadcast-to-N is one message per recipient under a bounded-concurrency queue — never a foreach-await loop
nodes.body: A handler iterating recipients and awaiting a sender per recipient holds the request open for N × latency, concentrates work on one process, and spikes the rest of the system. Publish one message per recipient (or batch of K), return immediately, and process under an explicit parallelism cap — the throttle gives natural back-pressure so fast producers can't starve slow consumers.
nodes.symptom: foreach (recipient) await sender.Send(...) inside a request or message handler
nodes.fix: per-recipient messages processed under a bounded-concurrency local queue

aliases: renamed the meter and lost the dashboard
triggers: Setting up OpenTelemetry metrics for our Wolverine-based messaging services.
Cleaning up the telemetry configuration and tidying the meter names in Program.cs.
Building a Grafana dashboard for dead-letter queue depth and message execution failures.
Adding custom counters for messages sent and received in our messaging handlers.
Messaging metrics disappeared from the dashboard after a small refactor of the OTel setup, no errors anywhere.
Prometheus shows zero series from our message framework even though the meter is registered.
ASP.NET request metrics show up fine but nothing from the messaging library ever reaches the collector.
OpenTelemetry meter name mismatch, instrumentation not exported, metrics silently missing
AddMeter not picking up a library's instruments, meter naming in .NET metrics
telemetry pipeline collecting nothing for one library, empty metrics with no error
nodes.title: Frameworks that suffix meter names need wildcard registration — the literal name silently collects nothing
nodes.body: Wolverine names its meter 'Wolverine:{ServiceName}', so telemetry must register AddMeter("Wolverine*"); a literal AddMeter("Wolverine") collects zero metrics with no error. Flag any 'tidying' of the wildcard to a literal. Corollary: prefer the framework's own instruments (DLQ depth, execution failures, sent/received, inbox/outbox depth) over hand-rolled equivalents — see the dead-metric lesson.
nodes.symptom: messaging metrics vanish from the dashboard after an innocuous meter-name cleanup
nodes.fix: keep the wildcard meter registration; lean on framework-emitted instruments

aliases: memory grows in a hosted service
one bad row stops the batch
triggers: Writing a BackgroundService that expires stale reservations every five minutes.
Adding a hosted job to purge old outbox rows, running on three replicas in Kubernetes.
Writing unit tests for a cleanup job whose behaviour depends on the current time.
Reviewing a cron-style worker that retries failed payments in a loop.
The nightly cleanup job's memory keeps growing until the pod gets OOMKilled.
Every replica ran the same expiry job and customers got the reminder email three times.
One malformed row threw an exception and the whole sweep stopped processing the rest.
background worker, hosted service, scheduled task, periodic job in .NET
DbContext lifetime in a long-running worker, scoped services captured by a singleton
cron job running on every replica, one-instance-only job in a scaled-out deployment
nodes.title: Background sweepers: fresh DI scope per iteration, no-wait distributed lock, injected clock, per-row exception isolation
nodes.body: Cron-style background jobs create a fresh DI scope per iteration (a reused scope accumulates every row in the change tracker), take a no-wait distributed lock when running cross-replica (released in await-using for exception safety), inject TimeProvider instead of DateTime.UtcNow for test determinism, and wrap each iteration in try/catch so one poison row can't kill the sweep.
nodes.symptom: sweep memory grows with table size, duplicate work across replicas, or one bad row aborts the run
nodes.fix: scope-per-iteration, no-wait lock, injected clock, per-iteration try/catch

aliases: mutate the entity from the handler
exposed List on a domain object
triggers: Modeling an Order entity with paid, shipped and cancelled states in the domain layer.
Refactoring an anemic domain model where command handlers set entity properties directly.
Reviewing a PR that exposes the order's line items as a public list on the entity.
Setting up the Domain project for a new bounded context and deciding what it may reference.
A handler set an order's status straight to Shipped even though it was never paid.
Someone added items to the cart's collection from outside and skipped the total recalculation.
The Domain project now references EF Core because someone added a RowVersion attribute.
DDD aggregate root design, encapsulation, rich domain model versus anemic model
state machine on an entity, guarded status changes, invariants enforced inside the entity
persistence ignorance, clean architecture domain layer free of infrastructure packages
nodes.title: Aggregate shape (when earned): validating factory, private setters, named transitions, read-only collections, zero dependencies
nodes.body: Entities are built via a validating static Create factory with private setters; state changes go through named transition methods (MarkAsPaid(), never Status = Paid) that throw on invalid transitions; collections expose IReadOnlyList over a private list, mutated only via named methods. The domain references nothing — no ORM, logging, or messaging; concurrency tokens live as shadow state in the persistence layer so the entity stays clean. (When the shape is earned at all — see the observed-invariant rule.)
nodes.symptom: public setters, direct property mutation from handlers, mutable exposed lists, or infra references in Domain
nodes.fix: factory + named transitions + read-only collections; shadow concurrency tokens

aliases: status check at the top of the handler
triggers: Writing a consumer for PaymentCompleted that marks the order as paid.
Handling at-least-once delivery from RabbitMQ in our order status message handlers.
Writing tests for a message handler that receives the same event twice.
Reviewing a consumer that relies on the entity throwing when a status change is invalid.
The dead-letter queue is full of messages that were just harmless redeliveries.
Duplicate events throw InvalidOperationException in the aggregate, get retried, then dead-lettered.
A late-arriving shipment event lands in the DLQ because the order is already completed.
idempotent consumer, dedupe, at-least-once semantics for message handlers
poison messages that are not really poison, false alarms on the dead letter queue
redelivery, duplicate delivery and out-of-order messages in an event-driven system
nodes.title: Idempotency lives at the handler (pre-check and no-op); the aggregate's throw is the backstop, not the guard
nodes.body: Consume handlers pre-check state before invoking the transition (if status isn't the expected precursor, return) so benign redeliveries no-op. The aggregate's throw-on-invalid-transition remains as the invariant backstop — but if the throw IS the guard, every duplicate or late delivery lands on the DLQ as a false poison message. Tests for these guards must state that a no-op, not a throw, is the intended behavior.
nodes.symptom: duplicate/late-delivered messages filling the DLQ via aggregate invariant throws
nodes.fix: status short-circuit at the top of the consume handler; aggregate throw as defense in depth

triggers: Adding an SMS sender alongside the existing email sender behind the same notification interface.
Registering two payment gateway implementations of one port and picking one per request.
Reviewing a PR that introduces a factory class for a storage service with a single implementation.
Wiring up dependency injection for a new notification channel in Program.cs.
Every notification goes out as SMS regardless of the Channel field on the message.
DI always resolves the last registered implementation and the other one is never called.
There is a SenderFactory with a switch statement that only ever returns one class.
strategy pattern with dependency injection, multiple implementations of one interface
service locator, factory pattern for choosing an implementation, abstract factory over the container
IEnumerable of services, picking an implementation at runtime, Autofac named registrations
nodes.title: Multi-impl ports route via keyed DI; premature factories and unrouted multi-registrations are twin failure modes
nodes.body: Two DI-registration bugs: (1) premature factory — a keyed/factory setup wrapping a port with exactly one implementation is speculative coupling; plain scoped registration is right until a second impl ships. (2) missing routing — with 2+ impls registered plain AND per-call selection intended (a Channel field picking the sender), DI silently returns the last-registered impl for every call, dropping the routing intent: a latent bug, not a style nit. Use the container's keyed-services API for routing — never a hand-rolled port factory, since the container IS the canonical factory.
nodes.symptom: every call routes to one impl regardless of the selector field, or an unused factory wraps a single impl
nodes.fix: one impl: plain registration. multiple + per-call selection: keyed services keyed by the routing value

aliases: test the handler against a real database
triggers: Writing tests for a new command handler that saves an order and publishes an event.
Deciding the test strategy for a service: what belongs in unit tests versus integration tests.
Reviewing a PR whose handler tests mock the repository and check that Save was called once.
Adding coverage for a handler with an authorization check and an idempotency short-circuit.
All tests pass with mocks but the handler fails against the real database.
Our handler has three branches but there is only one test, for the happy path.
Tests break every time we refactor because they assert on mock call counts.
Testcontainers, WebApplicationFactory, API tests against a real Postgres in Docker
mocking the repository with Moq and verifying it was called once, interaction-based tests
test pyramid versus testing trophy, which tier should cover command handlers
nodes.title: Integration tests are the default tier for handlers; unit tests are reserved for pure domain logic — and every guard branch gets a test
nodes.body: Any handler touching the DbContext is tested through the real API against real containers: hit the endpoint, assert DB state and tracked message envelopes — not mock-a-repository-and-count-calls. Unit tests cover pure logic only (transition guards, validation). A mock of a repository wrapper in a unit test signals two defects at once: the wrapper shouldn't exist and the test belongs in the integration tier. A handler with security guards, idempotency short-circuits, or ordering invariants needs a test per branch — one happy-path test on a three-branch handler is a finding.
nodes.symptom: handler tests mocking repositories and verifying call counts, or multi-branch handlers with one happy-path test
nodes.fix: move DbContext-touching tests to the integration tier; enumerate the missing branch scenarios

triggers: Adding a new GitHub Actions workflow to build and test the API on pull requests.
Writing a deploy workflow with several bash steps that pipe output through grep and tee.
Reviewing a PR that SHA-pins the actions in just one of our workflow files.
Hardening our CI pipelines after a supply-chain security review.
The CI step passed even though the test command inside the pipe failed.
A security scanner flagged that our checkout step leaves the GITHUB_TOKEN in the git config.
Old workflow runs keep going after I push new commits, wasting minutes and racing deploys.
GitHub Actions security best practices, token permissions scoped per workflow
bash strict mode in CI scripts, exit on error, pipe failures swallowed silently
unpinned third-party actions flagged by a scanner, superseded runs piling up in the queue
nodes.title: CI workflow baseline: pipefail, no persisted credentials, least-privilege permissions, concurrency groups — pin actions in one batch, not piecemeal
nodes.body: Every bash run block starts with set -euo pipefail; checkout sets persist-credentials false when the job doesn't push; every workflow declares explicit least-privilege permissions and a concurrency group cancelling superseded runs. Deliberately NOT a per-PR finding: individually unpinned @vN actions — SHA-pinning one workflow while others float is inconsistency theater, so pinning is a single repo-wide hardening pass.
nodes.symptom: a run block continuing past a failed pipe segment, or a read-only job persisting its checkout token
nodes.fix: apply the four baseline hardenings on every new workflow; batch SHA-pinning as one dedicated PR

triggers: Adding an OrderShipped integration event so the notification service can email the buyer.
Building a notification consumer that sends emails when orders change state.
Reviewing a change to an event contract that renames a field consumers use.
Designing cross-service event payloads for a new fulfilment service.
Order Shipped emails stopped going out, but the event is published and consumed without errors.
The notification handler only has an order ID and cannot work out which user to notify.
One event type is missing the BuyerId that all of its sibling events carry.
fat events versus thin events, what data an integration event payload should include
message contract versioning, backward compatible schema changes, breaking downstream consumers
push or email notification targeting, looking up who to notify from a domain event
nodes.title: Events that can trigger notifications must denormalize the recipient ID — an OrderId can never resolve to an inbox
nodes.body: Any cross-service event that triggers (or could trigger) a user-facing notification downstream carries the recipient identifier denormalized from the producing aggregate; a consumer keying a notification on an entity ID has a recipient-key-that-can't-resolve bug. Precedent: a dispatch event shipped without BuyerId while sibling events had it, silently breaking 'Order Shipped' emails. Contract changes are additive-only within a major version — add init-only properties, never remove or rename fields consumers bind to.
nodes.symptom: a notification consumer silently dropping messages because the event lacks a resolvable recipient
nodes.fix: add the denormalized recipient field additively; audit consumers for non-recipient keys

Swapping out our message broker library and updating the OpenTelemetry tracing setup.
Cleaning up Directory.Packages.props after dropping a dependency from the solution.

ActivitySource registration for distributed tracing, missing spans after a library change
Central Package Management leftovers, unused package versions in NuGet
nodes.found_by: .coderabbit.yaml ServiceDefaults/Extensions.cs (both bit the ASB→RabbitMQ swap, PR #159)
nodes.title: Removing a transport package leaves two silent orphans: dead telemetry source registrations and stranded central package versions
nodes.body: Deleting the PackageReference is not enough. Sweep for (1) a dead AddSource(...) for the removed transport's ActivitySource in the tracing block — it silently collects nothing and masks that the replacement's source may be missing — and (2) an orphaned PackageVersion in the central versions file with no remaining reference. Both bit the ASB-to-RabbitMQ swap.
nodes.symptom: messaging spans missing after a transport swap; stale central package versions
nodes.fix: pair every transport removal with a tracing-source and central-package sweep in the same PR

nodes.title: Audit verdict: captive-dependency rules held by habit only — enforce with ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild, not tribal knowledge
nodes.body: The DI-lifetimes audit found the project avoids captive dependencies (a singleton capturing a scoped service) purely by developer behavior — no ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild enforcement, no canon rule. The follow-up audit added the adjacent anti-pattern: resolving scoped services from the root provider instead of minting a scope. Lesson: lifetime discipline should be build-time-validated, not tribal.
nodes.symptom: a DI container with scope-validation off and no lifetime rules in canon
nodes.fix: enable ValidateScopes+ValidateOnBuild; encode the captive-dependency and root-provider rules

nodes.title: Audit verdict: audit an article's EXAMPLES, not just its stated advice — this one violated its own canon three times
nodes.body: An audit of a do/avoid microservices guide found all 10 stated items already covered by canon — but the article's own code examples contradicted it three times: publish-after-save dual-write instead of an outbox, audience validation disabled against the JWT rule, and a service-interface layer against the architecture. The audit also surfaced a recurring implicit stance the project practiced but never documented (internal-gRPC trust, no API gateway) — the second undocumented-stance find that day. Method lesson: examples are where an article's real teaching lives, and where it quietly contradicts itself.
